sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for?** No.
   - **Where:** The headline and subline (x 96–800, y 80–250) promise adult lessons. The two blocks below ("Join the lanes", "Family hour", x 96–985, y 355–435) offer open lane swimming and a children's session.
   - **What the viewer meets:** They can tell it's about swimming, but not whether this is a lesson sign-up or a pool's general timetable. They also can't tell whose pool it is or where it is, because no name or place appears anywhere.
   - **No next step:** Nothing on the page is clickable. A nervous adult who decides "yes, Tuesday" has no button or link and no time, price or "book a place".
   - **Why:** A page should tell users within seconds what it is, what they can do and where to click (Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*). A piece should also carry one main message, with secondary details clearly subordinate.
   - **Fix:** Make the Tuesday class the single message. Add one specific ask, such as "Book a Tuesday trial class", with the time and place next to it. Then either label the two lower blocks as "Also at [pool name]" so they read as secondary, or move them off this section.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.
2. **Do the colors, shapes, and directions of the piece carry the mood its message calls for?** No.
   - **Where:** The whole frame is near-black and mid-grey Inter on flat white. There is no colour, shape or image anywhere in the 1280×800, and the lower 40% (y≈450–800) is blank.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The copy is warm and reassuring ("a coach in the water beside you"), aimed at adults who may be anxious about water. The visual tone is neutral, like a default template or a settings page, so it does nothing to back up that reassurance or suggest water.
   - **Why:** Colour temperature, saturation and value should support the intended emotion (Itten, *The Art of Color*). Here they don't contradict the message; they just say nothing.
   - **Fix:** Bring in one cool, calm colour or a photo of an adult learner with a coach, so the look carries the "safe, supported" feeling the words promise. Use the empty lower band for it, or close the frame up.
   - **Type and weight:** Taste, minor.

**What's working.**
- **Clear headline:** "Learn to swim" is short, plain and dominant at about 90 px bold. It names the outcome the viewer wants, not the product, so the topic lands in under a second.
- **Specific subline:** "Small adult classes on Tuesday evenings, with a coach in the water beside you" says who, when and how in one line. "Coach in the water beside you" speaks straight to the fear an adult learner has.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (one-sentence purpose; colours and shapes carry the mood), 0 unsure.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No.
   - **Where:** Two text levels are almost the same size. The subhead "Small adult classes on Tuesday evenings…" (about x 96–795, y 195–250) looks about 22 px. The card titles "Join the lanes" and "Family hour" (x 96 and x 576, y≈367) look about 20 px. Neither one is bold. The subhead is grey and the titles are near-black, so the card titles end up pulling about as hard as the subhead. Each card title is also only about one size step above its own body text (about 16 px, grey, y 392–435).
   - **What the viewer gets:** After the headline, there is no clear second stop. The subhead, the two card titles and the card text read as one band of similar, light text. The page's real offer (adult classes on Tuesday evenings with a coach in the water) doesn't stand clearly above the two side programmes, so it is hard to tell the main offer from the extras. The card titles are regular weight and barely larger than their text, so they look like the first line of a paragraph rather than headings.
   - **Why:** Each level has to be distinguishable from the next at a glance (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*). A heading one size larger than its text looks like an accident, not a choice (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8). Sizes should come from a modest scale of distinct steps (Bringhurst, 3.1.1).
   - **Fix direction:** Make each level differ from the next in a way that is obvious at a glance, not by one step. Either make the subhead clearly larger than the card titles or give it more presence, so it is plainly level two. Make the card titles semibold or bold so they read as headings over their text, and move them clearly below the subhead in size. That gives a scale of about four sizes that don't collide: headline, subhead, card title, body.
   - **Type:** Defect. **Weight:** major. With only four text elements on the page, the step after the headline is most of the hierarchy, and it currently fails.

**What's working.**
- **The headline clearly dominates.** "Learn to swim" is about 90 px, heavy and near-black on white, roughly four times the size of anything else. The eye has one obvious place to start and knows straight away what the page is about. Keep that scale contrast when revising.
- **Card titles don't rely on size alone.** They are near-black over grey body text. Colour is the right second channel to keep when you add weight.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each level distinct from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same).

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** and **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** These two make one finding.
   - **Where:** All the content sits in the box x 96–985, y 80–435. Below y≈435 the whole band down to y 800 is empty, about 45% of the frame. To the right of x≈985 there is a strip about 295 px wide, three times the 96 px left margin.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The empty space is all in one place, which is good. But it has no shape and nothing sits against it, so it looks like the page stopped loading or the designer ran out of content, not like breathing room. All the weight, especially the heavy headline, is packed into the top-left quadrant, so the frame tips up and to the left. The bottom half carries no weight to balance it.
   - **Why:** Tschichold and Müller-Brockmann say empty space should be shaped on purpose, and that large unexplained empty areas are a fault. Ruder says the tension between printed and empty areas comes from contrast against something dense. Arnheim says a heavy side needs a counterweight.
   - **Fix:** Make the empty space look chosen. Either give the lower or right area something with weight (a picture of the pool, the class details, or the sign-up action), or rescale and reposition the block so the space around it has clear proportions. A third card would also pick up the 480 px column rhythm and fill the right strip.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.
2. **Does the arrangement lead the eye from the first element through the rest, with no line, gaze, or pointing shape that leads it off the edge?**
   - **Where:** The eye goes headline (y≈80–165) → subhead (y≈195–250) → "Join the lanes" → "Family hour" (x 576–985, y≈357–435), and then stops. Nothing comes after the second card, and the empty band below doesn't draw the eye onward.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The path just ends, with no final element (Arnheim and Dondis: no dead ends). The viewer has read about three offers and is left with nowhere to go. The headline promises "Learn to swim", but nothing in the arrangement leads to a place to act on it.
   - **Fix:** Put an end point on the path, such as a booking or sign-up action placed where the eye ends up: under the subhead or after the cards. The missing call to action itself probably belongs to the hierarchy or whole-piece critic. Here the finding is that the arrangement has no end point.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.

**What's working.**
- **One shared left edge:** The headline, subhead and first card all sit on x≈96, and the heavy "L" looks optically on the line. The two cards sit cleanly on a 480 px column step, and their headings (y≈367) and body lines (y≈400/424) share baselines. The page reads as one ordered column structure.
- **Spacing groups things correctly:** The headline-to-subhead gap is about 30 px, the gap from the subhead to the cards about 105 px, and each card heading sits about 10 px above its text. The hero and the cards read as separate groups, and each heading clearly belongs to its own text.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (empty space gathered and deliberate; visual weight balances; arrangement leads the eye through to an end)

Report written: the only Text problem is the loose spacing in the headline.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Are large headings set with tighter letter and word spacing than the text?** No. The headline "Learn to swim" (about x 96–696, y 85–160, roughly 100 px bold) looks set with the same letter and word spacing as the text. At that size the default spacing looks loose. The word gaps (about 25–30 px between "Learn", "to" and "swim") let the line split into three separate words rather than one solid phrase, and the letters in "Learn" sit slightly apart.
   - **Why:** Lupton, *Thinking with Type*, p. 80, says space between letters grows as type gets bigger, so large type needs fine-tuning. Bringhurst (2.1.1) and Hochuli (*Detail in Typography*, p. 34) say large sizes need proportionally less word space.
   - **Fix:** Tighten the headline's letter spacing slightly (about −0.02 em is typical for this kind of face at display sizes) and let the word spaces close up with it. Lupton warns against heavy negative tracking, so stop before the letters touch.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention, minor. The headline already reads at once, so this is polish, not a reading problem.

**What's working.**
- **Line length:** The subtitle wraps at about 66 characters and the card text at about 50. Both sit in the 45–75 range, so each line reads comfortably without a long eye jump back to the start.
- **Left edge:** The stem of the headline "L" lines up with the subtitle and the first card at x≈96. That gives the page one crisp left edge, and with this little on the page that edge is what holds it together.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (large headings set tighter than text).

First read: the eye lands on the big black "Learn to swim" heading at the top left, drops to the gray subtitle, then to the two small headed blurbs. It reads as the top of a landing page for a swim school or pool. It feels calm and plain, close to an unstyled wireframe. Job (my assumption): get adults to sign up for swim classes and tell visitors about the other pool sessions.

Walk, Color:
- Small palette: yes. One neutral range: near-black, a mid slate gray and white. No hue.
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes. There is none.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Near-black on white, with gray as the middle step, so the structure survives grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no hues to misplace.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The heading black and the card-title black match, and the subtitle gray and body gray match.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. Nothing is coded by color.
- Dark theme not pure black: yes. This is a light theme.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None of the checklist lines is a `no`. One point the checklist has no line for:

1. *(Not on the checklist)* **The page has no color of its own.** Everything is near-black, slate gray and white (1280×800). For a swim school, this leaves out the cheapest signal of what the page is about and whose page it is. A viewer gets no hint of water, pool or brand, and the two offers ("Join the lanes", "Family hour") look like plain text rather than places to go. The fix is one brand hue used sparingly, for example on the ask or the two offer headings, with the neutrals kept as the base. Taste. Weight: minor for color alone, though it adds to the generic, unfinished look the other sections may raise.

**What's working.** The neutral range is disciplined. There are two text tones on white: near-black for the heading and offer titles, mid gray for the supporting copy. Value alone does the ranking, so heading versus supporting text holds up in grayscale with no help from hue.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. There are no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks on the page. It is all type on white.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The bottom of the frame, from about y 440 to 800, is empty. So is the space to the right of the two cards, from about x 990 to 1280. Pictures that never loaded would leave gaps like these, with no broken-image icon or empty box. Load the live page to see whether a hero image or card images are meant to appear. If they are, the answer to "Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?" becomes no.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The image has no chart, table or numbers shown as data.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

**Section.** Interface: skipped. The image has no controls: no button, link, field, menu or navigation. The two card titles, "Join the lanes" and "Family hour", look like plain headings. They are dark text with no underline, arrow or border, so nothing marks them as links. (For the director: the page has no way to sign up or ask for a class time. That gap belongs under the whole-piece or hierarchy sections, not this one.)

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Interface: skipped
